description: The Covenants with Abraham and Moses at Sinai; the Messiah and the Messianic Age.
content_html:
What is a Covenant?

A Covenant is a solemn agreement or promise between G-d and the Jewish people. Unlike an ordinary contract, a covenant in Jewish tradition carries profound religious and moral weight: G-d makes promises to the people, and the people in turn commit to living according to G-d’s commands. Two covenants are particularly central to Jewish belief — the Covenant with Abraham and the Covenant at Sinai with Moses.

The Covenant with Abraham

Abraham is the founding patriarch of Judaism. In Genesis 12:1–3, G-d called Abraham to leave his homeland and travel to a new land, promising him: “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great.” G-d promised Abraham three things: a special relationship with G-d, many descendants (a great nation), and the Promised Land of Canaan.

The sign of this covenant was circumcision: every Jewish male was to be circumcised as a physical mark of the covenant relationship between G-d and Abraham’s descendants. This practice continues in Judaism today through the ceremony of Brit Milah. Isaiah 51:3 speaks of the Promised Land being made like the Garden of Eden, reinforcing the vision of blessing attached to the covenant. The covenant with Abraham established the Jewish people as a people chosen by G-d for a special purpose and relationship.

Key Fact

In the Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1–3), G-d promised: (1) a special relationship with G-d; (2) many descendants to become a great nation; (3) the Promised Land of Canaan. The covenant was sealed with circumcision as its sign.

The Covenant at Sinai and Moses

Moses is the most important prophet in Judaism. According to the Tenakh, G-d appeared to Moses on Mount Sinai and gave him the Torah, including the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2–14). This is known as the Covenant at Sinai — G-d promised to be the G-d of Israel and to protect the people, while the Israelites promised to keep G-d’s laws. The Torah became the basis of Jewish law and practice.

The Ten Commandments cover both the relationship between humans and G-d (such as having no other gods and keeping the Sabbath holy) and the relationship between human beings (such as prohibitions on murder, theft and dishonesty). Moses’ role as lawgiver and prophet makes him uniquely important in Judaism: no prophet before or after is regarded as having known G-d as directly as Moses did. The Covenant at Sinai is understood as making the whole Israelite people — not just their leaders — responsible for keeping G-d’s commands.

The modern State of Israel, established in 1948, is viewed in very different ways by different Jewish groups. Many Orthodox and Zionist Jews see it as the fulfilment of G-d’s promise of the Promised Land to Abraham (Genesis 12:1–3; Isaiah 11:11–12). Isaiah 11:11–12 speaks of G-d gathering the scattered people of Israel from the four corners of the earth — a verse often cited in relation to Jewish return to the land.

Some ultra-Orthodox Jews, however, believe that a Jewish state should only be established by the Messiah, not by human political action, and therefore reject the State of Israel on religious grounds. Progressive (Reform) Jews often interpret the Promised Land more symbolically — as a vision of a just and flourishing society — rather than a literal territorial claim. Ezekiel 37:24–28 envisions G-d’s servant dwelling among the people in the land forever, a passage interpreted differently across these traditions.

The Messiah

The word Messiah (Hebrew: mashiach) means “anointed one.” In ancient Israel, kings and priests were anointed with oil as a sign of divine appointment. Over time, Jewish belief developed the idea of a future Messiah — a great leader descended from the line of King David — who would bring an era of peace, justice and restored relationship between humanity and G-d.

The prophet Elijah is closely associated with the coming of the Messiah. Tradition holds that Elijah will return to announce the Messiah’s arrival. At Passover, Jews leave a cup of wine for Elijah and briefly open the door to welcome him as a symbolic expression of Messianic hope.

Key Fact

The Messiah is expected to: be descended from King David; be a political and spiritual leader; bring world peace; rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem; and gather the Jewish people from exile. Micah 4:1–3 describes a future age when “nation will not take up sword against nation.” Elijah is expected to return first to prepare the way.

The Messianic Age

The Messianic Age is the period of peace and perfection that will follow the Messiah’s coming. Micah 4:1–3 describes a time when nations will stream to Mount Zion to learn G-d’s ways, when swords will be beaten into ploughshares and warfare will cease. Isaiah 51:3 speaks of the Promised Land being comforted and made like the Garden of Eden, linking the Messianic Age with the restoration of paradise. Ezekiel 37:24–28 envisions a future in which G-d’s servant will reign over a united people living in the land, with G-d dwelling among them forever.

Orthodox Jews generally believe in a literal, personal Messiah — an individual human leader (not divine) descended from King David, who will restore the Temple, gather the exiled Jewish people and bring universal peace. This belief in a personal Messiah is central to traditional Jewish faith. Maimonides, the medieval Jewish philosopher, listed belief in the Messiah as one of his thirteen principles of faith.

Progressive (Reform) Jews often interpret the Messianic Age more collectively — as a future era of justice and peace that humanity will bring about through its own moral efforts, guided by Jewish values. In this view, the “Messiah” is less a specific individual and more a symbol of the human capacity to build a better world. Some Conservative and Masorti Jews hold positions between these two poles, accepting both individual and collective interpretations as valid.
exam_tip_html: When answering ‘Explain’ questions on the covenants, always specify which covenant you are discussing (Abraham or Sinai/Moses) and include at least one scripture reference (Genesis 12:1–3 for Abraham; Exodus 20:2–14 for Sinai). A common error is to confuse the Messiah with a divine figure — in Judaism the Messiah is human, not divine. For 15-mark ‘Discuss’ questions on the Messiah or the State of Israel, make sure you represent both Orthodox (personal, literal Messiah) and Progressive (collective, symbolic) views clearly, then weigh them and reach a justified conclusion. Accurate spelling of ‘Covenant,’ ‘Messianic,’ ‘Patriarch’ and ‘circumcision’ is rewarded on extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1–3) promised a special relationship with G-d, many descendants and the Promised Land of Canaan; its sign was circumcision. The Covenant at Sinai gave Moses the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2–14) as the basis of Jewish law.
  • The Messiah (Hebrew: mashiach, anointed one) is a future leader expected to bring peace, gather the Jewish people and restore the Temple; Elijah is associated with preparing the way. Orthodox Jews expect a personal Messiah; Progressive Jews often interpret this collectively.
  • The Messianic Age is a future era of global peace and harmony described in Micah 4:1–3 and Ezekiel 37:24–28. Jewish views on the State of Israel vary from seeing it as covenant fulfilment to rejecting it as requiring Messianic, not political, establishment.

practice_questions.text: State one promise G-d made to Abraham in the Covenant found in Genesis 12:1–3.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: a special relationship with G-d / many descendants (a great nation) / the Promised Land of Canaan [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of Moses in the Covenant at Sinai.
practice_questions.marks: Moses received the Torah and the Ten Commandments from G-d at Mount Sinai [1 mark]; he acted as the intermediary between G-d and the Israelite people, conveying G-d's laws and obligations to them [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews believe about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: The Messiah (Hebrew: mashiach) is an anointed leader descended from King David (1 mark); the Messiah will bring world peace and an end to warfare (e.g. Micah 4:1–3) (1 mark); the Messiah will gather the Jewish people from exile and rebuild the Temple (1 mark); Elijah is expected to return to announce the Messiah's arrival (1 mark); Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah whereas Progressive Jews may interpret this collectively (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Covenant with Abraham is significant for Jewish belief and practice today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The promise of the Promised Land (Genesis 12:1–3) continues to shape Jewish attitudes to the State of Israel — many Zionist Jews see the establishment of Israel in 1948 as the fulfilment of the covenant promise, supported by Isaiah 11:11–12 which speaks of G-d gathering scattered Israel.
• The sign of the covenant — circumcision — is still practised today in the ceremony of Brit Milah, marking Jewish male identity and continuity with Abraham.
• The covenant established the idea of the Jewish people as specially chosen by G-d, which shapes Jewish self-understanding as a people with a particular religious purpose and responsibility.
• The promise of descendants gives Jews confidence in G-d’s faithfulness across generations, sustaining Jewish identity through historical persecution.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per significance — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source]

practice_questions.text: 'The Covenant at Sinai is more important than the Covenant with Abraham for Jewish life today.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Ten Commandments from the Covenant at Sinai (Exodus 20:2–14) form the foundation of Jewish law and ethics, directly shaping how Jews live every day.
• The Sinai Covenant gave the whole Torah — 613 mitzvot — which regulates Jewish daily life far more comprehensively than the Abrahamic covenant.
• Moses is the greatest prophet in Judaism; the Sinai Covenant represents the defining moment of G-d’s revelation to the Jewish people as a whole.
• The weekly Shabbat, Jewish festivals and dietary laws all flow directly from the Sinai Covenant.

Arguments against:
• The Abrahamic Covenant established Jewish identity and the concept of chosenness before any law was given; without it, the Sinai Covenant would have no people to be given to.
• The promise of the Promised Land (Genesis 12:1–3) remains highly relevant today in relation to the State of Israel and Jewish homeland identity.
• Circumcision, the sign of the Abrahamic Covenant, continues to be practised by the vast majority of Jewish families across all denominations.
• The Abrahamic Covenant’s promise of descendants sustains Jewish hope for the future, including the coming of the Messiah from the line of David.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Exodus 20; Genesis 12; Micah 4:1–3; Isaiah 11:11–12), explicit weighing, justified conclusion that recognises both covenants as essential but may distinguish their different emphases.
Secure: Clear two-sided argument with some sources; reasoned conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources; simple conclusion.
Emerging: One perspective only; no sources; no clear conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

practice_questions.text: Outline different Jewish views on the nature of the Messiah and the Messianic Age.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a human leader from the line of David — who will restore the Temple and gather all Jews (1 mark); the Messianic Age will be an era of universal peace (Micah 4:1–3) (1 mark); Progressive Jews interpret the Messianic Age as a collective human achievement guided by Jewish values rather than the work of a single individual (1 mark); some ultra-Orthodox Jews reject the State of Israel because only the Messiah should establish a Jewish state (1 mark). [3 marks]

flashcard_questions.a: The land of Canaan, promised by G-d to Abraham and his descendants.

glossary_terms.definition: A binding agreement or promise between G-d and the Jewish people, with obligations on both sides.
The founding patriarch of the Jewish people, with whom G-d made a covenant promising descendants, land and a special relationship.
The land of Canaan, promised by G-d to Abraham and his descendants; significant in both ancient and modern Jewish identity.
The prophet and leader through whom G-d gave the Torah to the Jewish people at Mount Sinai.
The ten fundamental commandments given by G-d to Moses at Mount Sinai, recorded in Exodus 20:2–14.
From the Hebrew 'mashiach', meaning 'anointed one'; the future leader who Jews believe will bring peace and restore the Jewish people.
The prophet associated with announcing and preparing the way for the Messiah, according to Jewish tradition.
The future era of global peace, justice and harmony that will be ushered in by the Messiah, according to Jewish belief.
The modern Jewish state established in 1948, understood by many Jews as the fulfilment of the promise of the Promised Land.
